_note: WhatsDaf's own English renderings of the Hebrew commentaries on Sefaria (Vilna edition). Keys are <commentary>:<amud><segment>.<comment>. Square brackets are our clarifications. Very long Tosafot are condensed and marked "In brief".
rashi:a1.1: The upper kafatz: the upper knot, that is, the knee joint, where the shin and the thigh meet; and not the lower knot near the hooves.
rashi:a1.2: Corresponding to it, in a camel it is conspicuous: a camel has a bone that sticks out opposite the knee joint. So my teacher put it, in Shechitat Chullin. Another version I heard: for example, that a camel’s tail reaches that joint.
gershom:a1.1: That is, the upper kafatz: the upper joint.
gershom:a2.1: And corresponding to it, in a camel it is conspicuous: its leg joint, because it is very thick.
rashi:a4.1: And he proceeded to teach individual opinions: since we said above, “We did not hear of these,” only of the first ones he listed at Yavne, and then the tanna went on to blemishes taught not anonymously but in the name of individuals, such as Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus and Rabbi Ḥanina ben Gamliel, one might think the Rabbis disagree with them. That is why he went back and stated an unattributed ruling about them all: “For these blemishes one slaughters…”
gershom:a3.1: It states all of them anonymously for us: so that for those taught in the name of individuals too, one slaughters the firstborn.
rashi:a5.1: And one with warts: as we established above (40b), where the wart has no bone, since with a bone it is a full blemish; and where it has no hair, in the white of the eye. On the body it is mere hanging flesh.
rashi:a5.2: Garav and ḥazazit are kinds of boils.
gershom:a4.1: And the foul-smelling: whose sweat stinks.
rashi:a5.4: And with which a transgression was performed: it was the object of bestiality.
rashi:a5.5: Or that killed a person, on the basis of one witness: there is only one witness, whether to the bestiality or to the goring.
rashi:a5.6: On the basis of the owner: there is no witness, only the owner’s own statement. Had there been two witnesses, the animal would be stoned, and even benefit from it would be forbidden.
rashi:a6.1: A tumtum and a hermaphrodite: perhaps male, and then they are sacred; perhaps female, and then they are not.
rashi:a6.2: You have no blemish greater than that: this refers to the hermaphrodite. Its female organ counts as a blemish, so it is like a blemished firstborn: it is slaughtered in the country, and shearing it and working it are forbidden.
gershom:a11.1: Rabbi Yishmael says: You have no blemish greater than that, in a tumtum and a hermaphrodite, and it is slaughtered in the country. And the Rabbis say it is not a firstborn but may be shorn and worked, since a tumtum and a hermaphrodite are not sanctified as a firstborn.
rashi:a6.3: And the Rabbis say it is not a firstborn: since it is a creature of its own kind, and it may be shorn and worked.
rashi:a7.1: And is garav not a full blemish?
rashi:a7.2: But garav is written in the Torah (Leviticus 22:22), with “blind or broken,” where it says “or garav or yalefet.”
rashi:a7.3: And furthermore, is ḥazazit not a full blemish? But it is written in the Torah!
rashi:a7.4: This is ḥeres: a boil as hard as earthenware.
rashi:a7.5: The Egyptian ḥazazit: the boils brought upon the Egyptians.
tosafot:a7.1: [Our reading: “Garav, this is ḥeres.”] It is puzzling: why not raise the difficulty from the garav in the curses of Deuteronomy, “with garav and with ḥeres,” where garav is not ḥeres and is a permanent blemish, since it says “from which you cannot be healed”? One may answer that here the teaching builds upward: garav, which is ḥeres, dry inside and out, is a blemish, and even yalefet, moist outside and dry inside as explained below, is a blemish. And in the curses it also builds upward: he will be struck with garav, and even with ḥeres, which is harsher.
rashi:a7.6: Melapefet: it clings to him, as the Aramaic translation renders “and he joined” (Exodus 36) as ve-lapif.
gershom:a5.1: That it grabs him: that it holds on to him.
rashi:a10.1: Rather, there are three kinds of garav. The verse’s, among the blemishes, which we expound as “this is ḥeres”: dry inside and out.
rashi:a10.2: Egypt’s: that is the one in the curses, “and with garav and with ḥeres”: dry inside and moist outside. Since it is dry inside, it does not heal, and on a firstborn it would also be a full blemish.
rashi:a10.3: The mishna’s: moist inside and moist outside.
rashi:a10.4: Pore’aḥ, breaking forth: what shows on the surface, since something that sticks out “breaks forth.”
rashi:a10.5: And it is written avabu’ot: a word for flowing, implying that on the outside it was moist.
tosafot:a10.1: Rather, there are three: the verse about blemishes, which we expound as “this is ḥeres,” is dry inside and out; Egypt’s is moist outside and dry inside, and since it is dry inside it does not heal. If the Egyptians were healed of it, perhaps that was a miracle. One may wonder, though: what then is “the boil of Egypt” at the start of the verse of curses, if garav and ḥeres, which have no cure, are listed separately in that same verse?
gershom:a6.1: One does not slaughter for ordinary ḥazazit. The verse’s, which does not heal, is dry both inside and outside; Egypt’s is moist outside and dry inside, and it too does not heal; the mishna’s is moist both inside and outside, and it heals.
rashi:a11.1: From where are these matters derived: that one does not slaughter it in the Temple.
rashi:a11.2: From the flock, from the sheep: the verse in Leviticus, “And if his offering is from the flock, from the sheep or from the goats,” which we expound: “from the flock,” and not all of the flock; and so with each of them.
gershom:a7.1: To exclude the very old: even without a blemish, it is unfit to be offered.
rashi:a15.1: Ne’evad: an animal that was made into an object of idol worship.
rashi:a15.2: Muktze: set aside and separated for idol worship.
rashi:a15.3: Noge’aḥ: it gored a person, who died.
gershom:a8.1: Muktze: set aside for idol worship.
rashi:a16.1: And we ask, “But these are liable to death”: this refers to the animal that copulated with a person, the one that was the object of bestiality, and the one that gored.
gershom:a9.1: They are liable to death: the animal that copulated, the one copulated with, and the one that gored.
rashi:a16.2: And we answer: for example, where there is only one witness to the matter, or the owners admitted it themselves. Then the animals are not stoned, since one who admits to a liability that is a fine is exempt.
gershom:a10.1: Where there is only one witness, or the owner, since we do not put to death on their word.
rashi:a17.1: Perhaps it is a female: he would offer it as a firstborn without having consecrated it, and it is not sacred as a firstborn, so he would be bringing non-sacred animals into the Temple courtyard.
rashi:a18.1: And let one slaughter it on that account: since “cracked” is written in the Torah (Leviticus 22:22): “blind, or broken, or cracked.”
gershom:a12.1: Its female organ is a crack, and a crack is a blemish by Torah law.
gershom:a13.1: So too a crack must be in the location of a bone, and the crack of the female organ is in the location of flesh.
rashi:a20.1: Since the Master said “garav, this is ḥeres”: it is certainly a lesion that is cracked.
rashi:a20.2: And it is written, regarding lesions (Leviticus 13): “deep,” that is, low, like the sun’s appearance, which looks deeper and lower than the shade. So let the Torah write “crack,” which would imply that even in the location of flesh it is a blemish, though it is not repulsive like garav, and all the more so garav.
gershom:a14.1: Like the appearance of the sun, which looks deeper than the shade: so garav too [a later editor suggests reading: so garav, which is ḥeres, is also a crack]. The cracking of ḥeres implies a crack. That is why the Merciful One wrote garav: to say that garav is not disqualified as a crack, since garav is in the location of flesh, and a crack in the location of flesh is not a blemish, only in the location of a bone.
gershom:a15.1: No blemish greater than that: for if it is male, its female organ is a crack.
rashi:a23.1: Perhaps: we would also infer that a crack in the location of flesh is not a blemish only where the crack is not as noticeable as an animal’s female organ.
gershom:a16.1: He does not hold like Abaye, who compared “cracked” to “broken.” We do not say that; even in the location of flesh it is a crack. And he does not say like Rava, since here, though the crack of the female organ is in the location of flesh, it is a blemish because it is conspicuous.
rashi:b1.1: Or perhaps he is uncertain whether it is male or female, and when he says “with its blemish” he says it in the manner of “if you say”: if you say it may be a firstborn, it has its blemish with it.
gershom:b1.1: It is obvious to him: a hermaphrodite is not a creature of its own kind but a male, and a firstborn, and it comes with its blemish: the crack of the female organ.
gershom:b2.1: Or perhaps he is uncertain: perhaps it is a creature of its own kind and is not sacred.
gershom:b3.1: Or: if you say it is a firstborn, it comes with its blemish.
rashi:b2.1: To be flogged on its account, etc.: if you say it is a firstborn, he is flogged, since even a blemished firstborn may not be shorn or worked. If it is uncertain, we do not flog for an uncertainty.
rashi:b2.2: Alternatively, to give it to a priest: if it is a firstborn, he gives it to a priest, who eats it on account of this blemish. If it is uncertain, the Israelite owner eats it with this blemish, under the law of a doubtful firstborn, which its owner eats once it is blemished, since one who seeks to take from another must bring proof.
gershom:b4.1: To be flogged for shearing and labor, or to give it to a priest: if it is obvious to him that it is a firstborn with its blemish, one is flogged for shearing or working it, and is obligated to give it to a priest.
rashi:b3.1: Perhaps he said “if you say”: that is, if it is a firstborn, it comes with its blemish.
rashi:b4.1: Our reading, in Torat Kohanim: “A male, and not a female.” “Male” is written of a burnt offering from cattle, “he shall offer it, a male without blemish,” which implies: not a female.
rashi:b4.2: When it says “male” below: of a burnt offering from the flock.
rashi:b4.3: There is no need for the verse to state it: it is not needed for its plain sense, to exclude a female, since a female was already excluded.
rashi:b4.4: It comes to exclude a tumtum and a hermaphrodite.
gershom:b5.1: When it says “male” below: as it is written, “And if his offering is from the flock, from the sheep… a male without blemish.” There was no need to say it, since “male” was already said above, “If his offering is a burnt offering from the cattle,” and the verse already compared cattle to the flock.
rashi:b5.1: Whose is it: this exclusion of a tumtum and a hermaphrodite from the second “male.”
rashi:b5.2: If we say the first tanna of our mishna: for him a tumtum and a hermaphrodite are a case of uncertainty!
rashi:b5.3: And does a verse come to exclude an uncertainty? This is asked in surprise. Before Heaven there is no uncertainty; it must be excluding it because it is a creature of its own kind, which is not the first tanna’s view.
tosafot:b5.1: If we say the first tanna, for whom it is an uncertainty, does a verse come to exclude an uncertainty? You might ask: how do we know the first tanna’s reason is uncertainty? Perhaps it is like internal gums that were damaged or worn down, a blemish that bars slaughter in the Temple but does not permit slaughter in the country, while it is a definite firstborn. One may answer: since Rabbi Yishmael says in the baraita “it is a firstborn and its blemish is with it,” it follows that for the first tanna it is not a definite firstborn.
tosafot:b5.2: In brief: Tosafot explain why a verse cannot “exclude an uncertainty” here, although elsewhere the Torah does exclude doubtful cases (the doubtful tenth animal of tithe, 58b; a doubtful bright spot, Nazir 65b). A tumtum really is either male or female, so the Torah can set it aside while that is unknown; but the koy, the first shade of yellow, and the hermaphrodite are each one thing whose nature Heaven knows, so excluding them must mean they are a category of their own. They then reconcile this with Rav (Niddah 28a; Yevamot 83a), who treats a hermaphrodite as doubtful yet excludes it by a verse from entering the Temple: there the Torah wrote two exclusions, “from male to female,” one for the tumtum and one for the hermaphrodite. They go on to show how this fits Rav Ḥisda below, and why the Gemara’s later challenges from valuations and from the peace offering still stand. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
rashi:b6.1: Rather, the latter Rabbis of our mishna, for whom it is obvious that it is a creature of its own kind, who say: it is not a firstborn but may be shorn and worked.
gershom:b8.1: Rather, is it not for the latter Rabbis that the verse was needed? For them it is not an uncertainty but entirely non-sacred, since we said: And the Rabbis say it is not a firstborn and may be shorn and worked.
rashi:b6.2: Derive the tumtum, the hermaphrodite and the female from one “male,” since of a firstborn only one “male” is written, and from it they exclude all of them, tumtum and hermaphrodite, from a single “male.”
tosafot:b6.1: And they exclude all of them from it: all of them, the female, the tumtum and the hermaphrodite. And even for Rav Ḥisda below, who says to omit the tumtum, it says “all of them” because of the female and the hermaphrodite.
gershom:b9.1: If it is the Rabbis, why is another “male” needed? Derive it from one “male,” and all of them are excluded by it: female, tumtum and hermaphrodite.
rashi:b7.1: Rather, it is obvious that it is like Rabbi Yishmael: so we establish it, as we set out to explain, since we cannot establish it like those Rabbis; and it is obvious to him that it is a male.
rashi:b7.2: That is why it was needed to exclude: although it is a male, it is not sacred with any sanctity if one consecrated it as a burnt offering, and even shearing and labor are permitted. We could not derive this exclusion from sanctity from the first “male,” since of a firstborn only one “male” is written, and Rabbi Yishmael does not exempt it from the ban on shearing; because of the blemish he permits it only to be slaughtered.
rashi:b7.3: But if he is uncertain whether it is male or female, this baraita can no longer be established according to [Rabbi Yishmael], since a verse does not come to exclude an uncertainty. So whose view would it be?
tosafot:b7.1: In brief: Tosafot ask why, if Rabbi Yishmael holds a hermaphrodite is a blemished male, a verse is needed at all, since a blemished animal is already unfit for the altar. They quote Rashi’s answer (the verse teaches that it receives no sanctity, so even shearing and labor are permitted) and object that a blemish present from the start forbids shearing and labor only by rabbinic decree (14a). They cite another explanation of Rashi’s: the verse teaches that the female organ counts as a blemish though it is on flesh, against Abaye and Rava. Their own answer is that the verse shows it is worse than an ordinary blemished animal, which can still take effect as a substitute (temurah). Finally they explain why the Gemara does not attribute the baraita to other tanna’im who also treat the hermaphrodite as male. Open on Sefaria for the full text.
gershom:b10.1: Rather, it is obvious: the other “male” was needed for Rabbi Yishmael, for whom it is sacred as a firstborn. That is why it needed excluding: although it is sacred as a firstborn, it is not sacred as an offering.
rashi:b8.1: Actually, the latter Rabbis. And as for your “derive it from one verse,” since for a firstborn they derive it from one verse: not so, since of a firstborn two are written.
rashi:b8.3: “The males”: “that you shall have, the males shall be the Lord’s.”
tosafot:b8.1: “The male,” “the males”: you might ask that even without “the males” one could exclude a hermaphrodite from “the male,” as below regarding valuations, and in Niddah (28a) regarding a tumtum or hermaphrodite who saw white or red discharge. One may answer that perhaps there are other expositions, since many verses are written about the firstborn, such as “all your livestock that is male” (Exodus 34:19), and all are needed. And regarding the first chapter (9a), where “the males” is used for a different exposition, one may answer that that passage does not follow the latter Rabbis here.
gershom:b11.1: Actually, the latter Rabbis. And if you say that for them, since it is not sanctified as a firstborn, it should be derived from one “male”: indeed so. But of a firstborn two verses are written, “the male” and “the males,” and here too two “male”s are written.
rashi:b9.1: The dispute, where the latter Rabbis say it is a creature of its own kind, concerns the hermaphrodite.
rashi:b9.2: But a tumtum, all agree, is an uncertainty: it may not be shorn, and it is slaughtered neither in the Temple nor in the country.
tosafot:b9.1: In brief: Rav Ḥisda’s “a tumtum is sacred out of uncertainty” is not because “a verse does not exclude an uncertainty”; that principle does not apply to a tumtum, since some are male and some female. Rather, he does not see fit to apply the verse’s exclusion to a tumtum, which he regards as fully male or fully female. Rabbi Yoḥanan, who disagrees with him below, holds it is a creature of its own kind on which no sanctity takes effect even if it is found to be male. Tosafot add why the Gemara does not challenge Rav Ḥisda from Temurah 24b: Rav Ḥisda would explain that the owner’s declaration does not take effect on such offspring, but sanctity still falls on them at birth, like all offspring of consecrated animals.
gershom:b12.1: The dispute is about a hermaphrodite: for the latter Rabbis it is a creature of its own kind, and for the first tanna and Rabbi Yishmael it is a doubtful firstborn.
gershom:b13.1: But a tumtum: even for the latter Rabbis it is an uncertainty, since perhaps it will be torn open and found to be male, so it is sacred out of uncertainty.
rashi:b10.1: If that is so, since it is an uncertainty, then for valuations it should be valuated as a person, either by a man’s valuation or by a woman’s.
gershom:b6.1: If we say the first tanna, before Rabbi Yishmael: for him it is an uncertainty, since he said a tumtum and a hermaphrodite are slaughtered neither in the Temple nor in the country, because perhaps it is female and not a firstborn.
gershom:b7.1: And does a verse come to exclude an uncertainty? Before Heaven there is no uncertainty.
